mainTopic: Public needs on חול המועד: digging cisterns, and the sources for marking graves
overview: The גמרא reads our משנה closely: on חול המועד one may clean out public water cisterns, but not dig new ones. רבי יוחנן limits this. The ban on digging applies only when the public does not need the cisterns. After a back-and-forth over several ברייתות, the גמרא sorts them all by need. When cisterns are needed, an individual may clean his and the public may even dig. When they are not needed, the public may not dig and an individual may not even clean. רב אשי then proves from the word "כל" in the משנה that digging for public needs is allowed. Next the גמרא turns to marking graves. רבי שמעון בן פזי finds a hint in יחזקאל, and many other אמוראים bring other פסוקים that teach the same idea: warn people away from danger and טומאה. רבי יהושע בן לוי draws a lesson about weighing one's ways, and a story about רבי ינאי's student begins, continuing on the next amud.

steps.title: Reading the משנה: cleaning out is allowed, digging is not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about fixing public water cisterns and learns from its wording that only cleaning out (חטיטה) is allowed, not digging new (חפירה).
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says one may fix damaged water cisterns in the public area. From this we learn: cleaning them out, yes; digging new ones, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה and draws a close reading from it. It says that only cleaning out old cisterns is allowed on חול המועד, and digging new ones is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only talks about fixing cisterns that already exist and have been damaged. So the גמרא concludes that removing dirt from an old cistern (חטיטה) is allowed, while making a brand new one (חפירה) is not. This reading sets up the next step, which limits it.

keyTerms.meaning: Damaged water places (cisterns that need fixing)
Cleaning out: removing dirt and sediment from an existing pit

phrases.english: The damaged water cisterns in the public domain, etc.
Cleaning out — yes,
digging — no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the discussion by quoting the משנה and inferring a rule from its wording.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On חול המועד one may clean out existing public cisterns, but may not dig new ones.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: if the public needs it, even digging is allowed
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב quotes רבי יוחנן: the ban on digging applies only when the public does not need the cisterns. When they do need them, digging is allowed too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב said in the name of רבי יוחנן: The ban on digging was taught only when the public does not need the cisterns. But if the public needs them, even digging new ones is allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן limits the rule we just learned. Digging is forbidden only when the public does not need the cisterns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 sounded like digging is always forbidden. רבי יוחנן says that is only true when there is no public need. When the public needs water, even making a new cistern is allowed on חול המועד.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this when... (a phrase that limits a rule)

steps.whyThisMatters: This step creates the key line between public need and no public need. The rest of the sugya tests that line.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ya'akov said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין רַבִּים צְרִיכִין לָהֶם,
phrases.english: They taught this only when the public does not need them,
phrases.notes: 'This' means the rule from step 1 that digging is not allowed.

phrases.english: but if the public needs them —
even digging is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין רַבִּים צְרִיכִין לָהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the reading of the משנה from step 1 to cases with no public need.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Digging new cisterns on חול המועד is forbidden only when the public does not need them. When the public needs them, digging is permitted.

steps.title: A ברייתא forbids digging public cisterns
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן from a ברייתא that says one may not dig cisterns, ditches, or caves even for the public. That seems to mean digging is forbidden even when the public needs them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is digging really allowed when the public needs it? But a ברייתא teaches: One may clean out cisterns, ditches, and caves of a private person, and of course those of the public. But one may not dig cisterns, ditches, and caves of the public, and of course not those of a private person. Isn't this talking about a case where the public needs them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי יוחנן's rule. It quotes a ברייתא that forbids digging public cisterns, which sounds like a case where the public needs them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lets cleaning out go further, to private pits, and holds digging back even for public pits. If public pits were usually ones the public needs, the ברייתא would forbid digging even when there is public need, which goes against רבי יוחנן. The question 'מאי לאו' suggests that this is the plain reading.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it really permitted? (a doubting question)
But it was taught in a ברייתא
Cisterns, ditches, and caves: different kinds of pits for holding water
Needless to say, all the more so
Isn't it that...? (pushes a reading of a source)

steps.confusionAlert: The two 'needless to say' lines go in opposite directions. For cleaning out, private is allowed, so public surely is. For digging, public is forbidden, so private surely is. Public needs are treated as more important in both lines.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי רַבִּים צְרִיכִין לָהֶם מִי שְׁרֵי?
phrases.english: And when the public needs them, is it permitted?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתַנְיָא: חוֹטְטִין בּוֹרוֹת שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת שֶׁל יָחִיד,
phrases.english: But isn't it taught: One may clean out cisterns, ditches, and caves of an individual,
and needless to say, those of the public,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין חוֹפְרִין בּוֹרוֹת שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת שֶׁל רַבִּים,
phrases.english: but one may not dig cisterns, ditches, and caves of the public,
and needless to say, those of an individual.
What, is it not where the public needs them?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי רַבִּים צְרִיכִין לָהֶם מִי שְׁרֵי? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's rule from step 2 using a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's rule that digging is permitted when the public needs the cisterns.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא forbids digging public cisterns, and public cisterns seem to be ones the public needs. So digging would be forbidden even with public need.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about pits the public does not need
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about public pits that the public does not need. So it does not go against רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the ברייתא is talking about a case where the public does not need them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי יוחנן. It says the ברייתא's ban on digging public pits is only for pits the public does not need.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Something can belong to the public without the public needing it right now. By reading the ברייתא as a no-need case, it fits רבי יוחנן's line exactly: no need means no digging, and need means digging is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: No: a rejection of the suggested reading

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, on חול המועד digging new public cisterns is allowed only when the public needs them. For now, the ברייתא that forbids digging public pits is read as being about pits the public does not need. The next steps test this answer.

phrases.english: No, it is where the public does not need them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3 by limiting the ברייתא to a no-need case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case of the source (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's public pits are ones the public needs, so digging would be forbidden even with public need.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about public pits the public does not need, so רבי יוחנן's rule stands.

steps.title: The answer causes a problem for the individual's cisterns
steps.stepSummary: If the first ברייתא is talking about cisterns that are not needed, then its permission to clean an individual's cisterns would also be about unneeded cisterns. But another ברייתא says an individual may not clean them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Following the same logic for an individual, the ברייתא would be about a case where the individual does not need the cisterns. But is cleaning allowed then? A ברייתא teaches: for cisterns, ditches and caves of an individual, you may collect water into them, but you may not clean them out or plaster their cracks. For the public's cisterns, you may clean them out and plaster their cracks.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer it just gave in step 4. It points out that this answer makes the first ברייתא clash with a different ברייתא about an individual's cisterns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 4 the גמרא said the first ברייתא is about cisterns that are not needed. The same ברייתא also allowed cleaning an individual's cisterns, so that permission would have to be about unneeded cisterns too. But a second ברייתא says an individual may not clean his cisterns, so the step 4 answer does not hold up.

keyTerms.meaning: Following the same pattern; the matching case
Plastering or smoothing over their cracks

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not attacking רבי יוחנן directly here. It is attacking the answer from step 4, by looking at the other half of that same first ברייתא, the half about an individual.

phrases.english: Then in the matching case of an individual,
it would be where the individual does not need them.
Is cleaning them out allowed then?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתַנְיָא: בּוֹרוֹת שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת שֶׁל יָחִיד —
phrases.english: But it was taught in a ברייתא: cisterns, ditches and caves of an individual,
you may collect water into them,
but you may not clean them out
and you may not plaster their cracks.
And those of the public, you may clean them out
and plaster their cracks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 4 by applying its case-setting to the individual's half of the first ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 4 that the first ברייתא is about cisterns the public does not need.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the whole first ברייתא is about unneeded cisterns, then its permission to clean an individual's cisterns is also about unneeded cisterns. A second ברייתא forbids an individual to clean his cisterns, so the two ברייתות would clash.

steps.title: Reading it the other way causes a problem for the public's cisterns
steps.stepSummary: If instead the first ברייתא is about needed cisterns, then its ban on digging for the public would also be about needed cisterns. But a third ברייתא allows the public to dig when they need them. So the first ברייתא is still a problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what will you say, that it is talking about when the individual needs them? Then in the matching case of the public, it would be when the public needs them. But is digging forbidden then? A ברייתא teaches: for cisterns, ditches and caves of an individual, you may collect water into them and clean them out, but you may not plaster their cracks, fill in earth into them, or coat them with lime. For the public's, you may dig them and coat them with lime. So the first ברייתא is a problem!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the opposite reading, that the first ברייתא is about cisterns that are needed. It shows that this reading also clashes with a ברייתא, so the first ברייתא stays difficult.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the first ברייתא is about needed cisterns, its line forbidding digging for the public would mean digging is forbidden even when the public needs it. But a third ברייתא says the public may dig and coat cisterns with lime, which would be when they need them. Neither reading seems to work, and the גמרא says outright that the first ברייתא is difficult.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, what will you say? (testing the other option)
Coating them with lime so they hold water
That first one, meaning the first ברייתא

phrases.english: Rather, what? That it is when the individual needs them?
Then in the matching case of the public,
it would be when the public needs them.
Is digging forbidden then?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָתַנְיָא: בּוֹרוֹת שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת שֶׁל יָחִיד —
phrases.english: But it was taught in a ברייתא: cisterns, ditches and caves of an individual,
you may collect water into them and clean them out,
but you may not plaster their cracks,
and you may not clear earth into them,
phrases.notes: This is not the same as cleaning them out. Here it means pushing earth into the cracks to fill them.

phrases.english: and you may not coat them with lime.
And those of the public, you may dig them
and coat them with lime!
So that first ברייתא is a problem!
phrases.notes: He means the ברייתא from step 3, which said you may not dig even for the public.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries the opposite case-setting after step 5 knocked down the first one, and finds that it fails as well.
steps.kashyaTarget: The first ברייתא (step 3), read as being about cisterns that are needed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the first ברייתא is about needed cisterns, then its ban on digging for the public applies even when the public needs them. A third ברייתא allows the public to dig, so the first ברייתא contradicts it.

steps.title: Re-reading the first ברייתא: when the cisterns are needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-reads the permission part of the first ברייתא as being about needed cisterns. An individual may clean his, and the public may certainly clean theirs, since they may even dig.
steps.simpleTranslation: Answer it like this: you may clean out an individual's cisterns when the individual needs them. And there is no need to say you may clean the public's cisterns when the public needs them, since even digging is allowed then.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem by splitting the first ברייתא into two cases. This first part explains the case where the cisterns are needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two halves of the first ברייתא do not have to describe the same situation. The permission to clean is about needed cisterns. In that case an individual may clean, and the public may go further and dig. This fits the ברייתא from step 6.

keyTerms.meaning: Answer it this way; explain it like this
There is no need to say; it is obvious

phrases.english: Answer it like this:
You may clean out an individual's cisterns
when the individual needs them,
and there is no need to say the public's
when the public needs them,
since even digging is allowed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the problem raised at the end of step 6 by re-reading the first ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the ברייתא as covering two different situations: needed and not needed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought every line of the first ברייתא described the same situation, either all needed or all not needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The permission line is about needed cisterns. An individual may clean, and the public may even dig.

steps.title: Re-reading the first ברייתא: when the cisterns are not needed
steps.stepSummary: The ban line of the first ברייתא is about unneeded cisterns. The public may not dig, and an individual may not even clean. Now all the ברייתות and רבי יוחנן fit together.
steps.simpleTranslation: And you may not dig cisterns, ditches and caves of the public when the public does not need them. And there is no need to say this about an individual, since when an individual does not need them, even cleaning them out is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer by explaining the second case, when the cisterns are not needed. This settles all the sources.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban on digging even for the public is about cisterns the public does not need, just as step 4 said. In that same situation an individual may not even clean, which fits the ברייתא from step 5. So רבי יוחנן's rule holds: need decides what is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Long, narrow ditches for holding water
Caves or covered pits for storing water

steps.whatToRemember: Needed: an individual may clean, and the public may even dig. Not needed: the public may not dig, and an individual may not even clean. This matches רבי יוחנן.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that, for both the individual and the public, what decides the rule on חול המועד is whether the work is actually needed.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין חוֹפְרִין בּוֹרוֹת שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת שֶׁל רַבִּים —
phrases.english: And you may not dig cisterns, ditches and caves of the public
when the public does not need them,
and there is no need to say an individual's,
since when an individual does not need them,
even cleaning them out is also forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין חוֹפְרִין בּוֹרוֹת שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת שֶׁל רַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer begun in step 7 by explaining the ban line of the first ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the ban line as being about unneeded cisterns.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ban on digging even for the public seemed to apply even when the public needs the cisterns, against רבי יוחנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban is only when the cisterns are not needed. In that case an individual may not even clean, which fits all the ברייתות and רבי יוחנן.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All the sources agree once we sort them by need: needed means more is allowed, not needed means less is allowed, and the public always gets more room than an individual.

steps.title: רב אשי's proof from the word "all" in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the משנה's phrase "all public needs" uses the extra word "כל" to include digging cisterns for the public.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Our משנה's wording also shows this. It says, "One may do all the needs of the public." What does the word "all" add? Doesn't it add digging?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי brings support from our משנה for the conclusion that the public may dig cisterns it needs on חול המועד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה could have simply said "public needs." The extra word "כל" must be adding something not written. רב אשי suggests the added item is digging new cisterns.

keyTerms.meaning: Is precise; its exact wording shows something

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Our Mishnah is also precise and shows this,
for it teaches: One may do all the needs of the public.
What does the word "all" come to include?
Does it not come to include digging?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: מַתְנִיתִין נָמֵי דַּיְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ברייתות were reconciled, רב אשי adds support from the משנה itself.
steps.raayaObject: That the public may dig cisterns it needs on חול המועד
steps.raayaSupportSource: The extra word "כל" in the משנה's phrase "עושין כל צורכי רבים"

steps.title: "All" may add the road and ritual bath repairs instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back. "כל" may add the public jobs listed in a ברייתא: clearing roads, fixing streets, and measuring and filling מקואות. That ברייתא also teaches that leaders who neglect these jobs are blamed for blood spilled.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It comes to include what was taught in a ברייתא: They go out to clear thorns from the roads, to fix the streets and highways, and to measure the ritual baths. If any ritual bath does not have forty סאה, they channel water into it until it has forty סאה. And how do we know that if they did not go out and do all this, any blood spilled there is counted against them as if they spilled it? The verse says: "And blood will be upon you."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects רב אשי's proof. It says the word "כל" could be adding a different list of public jobs taught in a ברייתא, not digging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If "כל" can be explained by other items, it no longer proves that digging is allowed. The ברייתא lists road clearing, street repair, and fixing מקואות. It adds a strong reason these jobs matter: neglecting them makes the leaders responsible for any deaths.

keyTerms.meaning: Forty סאה, the minimum amount of water for a kosher מקוה
They channel or direct water in
The verse teaches; introduces a פסוק as the source

steps.confusionAlert: The part about spilled blood is still part of the same ברייתא. It is not a new argument by the גמרא. It explains why these public repairs are so important.

phrases.english: No, it comes to include what was taught in a Baraita:
They go out to clear thorns from the roads,
and to fix the streets and the highways,
and to measure the ritual baths.

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל מִקְוֶה שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ אַרְבָּעִים סְאָה
phrases.english: And any ritual bath that does not have forty se'ah,
they channel water into it until it has forty se'ah.

phrases.aramaic: וּמִנַּיִן שֶׁאִם לֹא יָצְאוּ וְעָשׂוּ כׇּל אֵלּוּ,
phrases.english: And how do we know that if they did not go out and do all these,
any blood that is spilled there

phrases.aramaic: מַעֲלֶה עֲלֵיהֶם הַכָּתוּב כְּאִילּוּ הֵם שְׁפָכוּם —
phrases.english: is counted against them by the verse as if they had spilled it?
The verse says: "And blood will be upon you."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב אשי's proof by offering another meaning for the word "כל".
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from the word "כל". It does not reject the ruling itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: "כל" can be explained as adding the public repairs from the ברייתא, so it does not have to mean digging.

steps.title: Those repairs are already written in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the pushback. The משנה already lists roads, streets, and מקואות openly, so "כל" cannot be adding them. It must be adding digging.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the משנה teaches these openly: "And they fix the roads, the streets, and the ritual baths." So what does "one may do all the needs of the public" add? Doesn't it add digging?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the rejection from the last step. It shows that the ברייתא's jobs are already written in the משנה itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An extra word cannot be coming to add something the משנה already says in plain words. Since roads, streets, and מקואות are already listed, "כל" must be adding something new. That brings back רב אשי's reading: digging.

phrases.english: But it teaches these openly:
phrases.notes: "It" is our משנה, which already lists these repairs in its own words.

phrases.english: "And they fix the roads
and the streets and the ritual baths."

phrases.aramaic: וְעוֹשִׂין כׇּל צוֹרְכֵי רַבִּים לְאֵתוֹיֵי מַאי —
phrases.english: So what does "and one may do all the needs of the public" come to include?
Does it not come to include digging?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection in step 10 and brings back רב אשי's proof from step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 10 that "כל" adds the ברייתא's road and ritual bath repairs
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה already names those repairs openly, so an extra word cannot be needed to add them. "כל" must add something not listed, which is digging.

steps.title: Conclusion: the משנה allows public digging
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that the proof stands. The משנה's word "כל" includes digging cisterns the public needs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא agrees that רב אשי's proof works and closes the discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other explanation for "כל" failed, so the only remaining meaning is digging. The משנה itself supports the earlier ruling that the public may dig cisterns it needs on חול המועד.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it; the proof is accepted

steps.whatToRemember: The public may dig new cisterns it needs on חול המועד. The משנה hints at this with the word "כל" in "עושין כל צורכי רבים", because the other public repairs are already listed openly.

phrases.english: Learn from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the argument of step 11 and confirms רב אשי's proof.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The word "כל" in the משנה includes digging cisterns that the public needs, so such digging is allowed on חול המועד.

steps.title: A hint for marking graves from יחזקאל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling that graves may be marked. רבי שמעון בן פזי finds a hint for this in a פסוק in יחזקאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: one may mark the graves. רבי שמעון בן פזי said: where is there a hint in the Torah for marking graves? The פסוק says: 'And he will see a human bone and build a sign next to it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic from the משנה, marking graves, and רבי שמעון בן פזי gives a source for it from a פסוק in יחזקאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Graves are marked so people walking by will know to stay away and not become טמא. רבי שמעון בן פזי calls his source only a 'רמז', a hint, not a full command. Here 'תורה' is used loosely to include the books of the prophets.

keyTerms.meaning: A hint, a source that points to a law without stating it outright

phrases.english: One may mark the graves.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi said:
A hint for marking graves
from the Torah, where is it?
The verse says:
"And he will see a human bone
and build a sign next to it."

steps.triggerLanguage: רֶמֶז לְצִיּוּן קְבָרוֹת מִן הַתּוֹרָה מִנַּיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה after the discussion of digging cisterns ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Marking graves is hinted at in יחזקאל 39:15: 'and build a sign next to it.'

steps.title: How could people know this before יחזקאל?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רב אשי: before יחזקאל lived, who taught that graves must be marked?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: But before יחזקאל came, who said this?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא challenges the source from יחזקאל, because people must have marked graves long before this prophet lived.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the law comes only from יחזקאל, then before him nobody would have had a source for it. That seems impossible, since people always cared about avoiding טומאה. So how can יחזקאל be the source?

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
But before Ezekiel came,
who said it?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא מִקַּמֵּי דְּלֵיתֵי יְחֶזְקֵאל, מַאן אֲמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the source just brought in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמעון בן פזי's use of a פסוק in יחזקאל as the source for marking graves.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A later prophet cannot be the first source for a law that must have been kept before his time.

steps.title: רב אשי points to the same problem with רב חסדא's teaching
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers by showing that the same question would hit רב חסדא, who also learned a law from יחזקאל: that an uncircumcised person may not serve in the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to your reasoning, what about what רב חסדא said: 'This matter we did not learn from the Torah of משה רבינו; we learned it from the words of יחזקאל בן בוזי: Any stranger, uncircumcised of heart and uncircumcised of flesh, shall not come into My Sanctuary to serve Me.' Before יחזקאל came, who said it?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי begins his answer by showing that רבינא's question would also apply to another accepted teaching. This sets up his real answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא openly says the rule about uncircumcised כהנים comes from יחזקאל, not from the Torah of משה. Yet כהנים surely followed this rule before יחזקאל. So רבינא's question is not special to marking graves, and it needs a general answer.

keyTerms.meaning: And according to your reasoning (turns the question back on the asker)
A stranger; here, one who has turned away from ה׳
To serve Me (in the בית המקדש)

phrases.english: And according to your reasoning,
what about that which Rav Chisda said:
This matter, from the Torah of Moshe our teacher
we did not learn;
from the words of Ezekiel ben Buzi we learned:
"Any stranger, uncircumcised of heart
and uncircumcised of flesh,
shall not come into My Sanctuary to serve Me"
Before Ezekiel came, who said it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רבינא's question by showing that it applies equally to a well-known teaching of רב חסדא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-question from a parallel case, leading into a general answer
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A law first written by יחזקאל could not have been known before him.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since רב חסדא's case has the same problem, there must be a general explanation, which comes in the next step.

steps.title: An old tradition that יחזקאל attached to a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: Both laws were known as a tradition from long before. יחזקאל came later and connected them to a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, they learned it as a tradition, and יחזקאל came and attached it to a פסוק. Here too: they learned it as a tradition, and יחזקאל came and attached it to a פסוק.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives his answer: these laws were known all along as a tradition, and יחזקאל only found a פסוק to hang them on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The law did not begin with יחזקאל. It was passed down by word of mouth, and יחזקאל gave it a written support in a פסוק. That is why רבי שמעון בן פזי called it only a 'רמז', a hint.

keyTerms.meaning: They learned it as a tradition passed down
He attached it to a פסוק (gave it support from a verse)

steps.whatToRemember: A law can be an old tradition from long ago, and a later prophet like יחזקאל may only attach it to a פסוק. The פסוק is a support, not the law's beginning.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think יחזקאל made up a new law. A prophet cannot add new laws; he only connected a law that was already known to a verse.

phrases.english: Rather, they learned it as a tradition
and Ezekiel came
and attached it to a verse.
Here too:
they learned it as a tradition,
and Ezekiel came and attached it to a verse.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא גְּמָרָא גְּמִירִי לַהּ וַאֲתָא יְחֶזְקֵאל וְאַסְמְכַהּ אַקְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רב אשי's answer that began with the parallel in step 15.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Marking graves was a known tradition from before יחזקאל, and his פסוק is only a support for it.

steps.title: רבי אבהו's source: impurity must call out
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו brings a source from the Torah itself: the מצורע calls out 'טמא טמא', which teaches that impurity must warn people to stay away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: from here: 'And he shall call out: Impure, impure.' Impurity calls out to him and tells him, 'Stay away.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו gives a different source for marking graves, this time from the Torah of משה, in the laws of the מצורע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מצורע must announce that he is טמא so others can avoid him. רבי אבהו learns a general rule from this: a source of טומאה must warn people away. A grave marker does the same job, so marking graves is rooted in this פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: And he shall call out: Impure, impure (said about the מצורע)

phrases.english: Rabbi Abahu said: from here:
"And he shall call out: Impure, impure"
Impurity calls out to him
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the person passing by, who might touch the טומאה.

phrases.english: and tells him, "Stay away."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second source for marking graves, in place of the פסוק from יחזקאל in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: The law that graves must be marked.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ויקרא 13:45, 'וטמא טמא יקרא': impurity must announce itself and warn people to stay away.

steps.title: רבי עוזיאל says the same idea
steps.stepSummary: רבי עוזיאל, grandson of רבי עוזיאל רבה, teaches the same lesson: impurity calls out and says 'stay away'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so said רבי עוזיאל, grandson of רבי עוזיאל the Great: impurity calls out to him and tells him, 'Stay away.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up רבי אבהו by showing that another sage taught the same idea in the same words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is added to the law. The point is support: רבי אבהו's reading of the פסוק was also taught by רבי עוזיאל.

keyTerms.meaning: And so said (introduces a sage who agrees)
The Great (the older sage of the same name)

phrases.english: And so said Rabbi Uzziel
grandson of Rabbi Uzziel the Great:
Impurity calls out to him
and tells him, "Stay away."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן אָמַר רַבִּי עוּזִּיאֵל בַּר בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי עוּזִּיאֵל רַבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי אבהו's teaching from step 17 with the same words from another sage.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אבהו's lesson that impurity must warn people away.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The same teaching from רבי עוזיאל, grandson of רבי עוזיאל רבה.

steps.title: The מצורע's call is needed for a different lesson
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the פסוק 'וטמא טמא יקרא' really comes to teach warning people about טומאה, since a ברייתא uses it to teach that the מצורע shares his pain so others will pray for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this פסוק really come to teach that? It is needed for what a ברייתא teaches: 'And he shall call out: Impure, impure.' He must let the public know of his pain, and the public will pray for mercy for him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אבהו's proof from the previous steps. It says the פסוק about the מצורע calling out is already used for another lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבהו used 'טמא טמא' to show that טומאה must warn people to stay away. A ברייתא reads the same words differently: the מצורע announces his suffering so that people will daven for him. If the פסוק is busy with that lesson, it cannot also be the source for warning people.

keyTerms.meaning: Does this come for this purpose? (a challenge that the source is needed for something else)
It is needed for (a different lesson)
As was taught in a ברייתא

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not doubting that the מצורע calls out 'טמא טמא'. It only asks what lesson that call is meant to teach.

phrases.english: But does this verse come for this purpose?
That verse is needed for what was taught in a ברייתא:
"And he shall call out: Impure, impure."
He must let the public know of his pain,
and the public will pray for mercy for him!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַאי לְהָכִי הוּא דַּאֲתָא? הַהוּא מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְכִדְתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the source רבי אבהו brought in step 17
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבהו's proof from 'וטמא טמא יקרא' that טומאה must warn people away
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק already used for one lesson (announcing pain so others pray) cannot be assumed to teach a second lesson.

steps.title: The double word 'טמא' teaches both lessons
steps.stepSummary: If the פסוק only taught one lesson, one 'טמא' would be enough. Since it says 'טמא טמא', we learn two lessons.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let the Torah write 'And he shall call out: Impure.' Why does it say 'Impure, impure'? Learn two things from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The extra word 'טמא' shows that the פסוק teaches two lessons, not one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One 'טמא' would have been enough for the lesson about davening for the מצורע. The second 'טמא' is extra, so it adds the second lesson: warn people to stay away from טומאה. This saves רבי אבהו's proof.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it write (the Torah could have written it shorter)

steps.whatToRemember: 'טמא טמא' teaches two things: the מצורע shares his pain so people will pray for him, and טומאה must warn people to stay away.

phrases.english: If so, let it write: "And he shall call out: Impure,"
why does it say "Impure, impure"?
Learn two things from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra word in the פסוק teaches an additional lesson
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק teaches only the lesson about sharing pain, so it cannot be a source for warning people.
steps.terutzMaskana: The repeated 'טמא' teaches both lessons, so רבי אבהו's proof stands.

steps.title: אביי: Do not put a stumbling block before the blind
steps.stepSummary: אביי brings a different source for marking graves: 'Do not put a stumbling block before the blind.'
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: The source is from here: 'Do not put a stumbling block before the blind.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי offers a new פסוק as a source for marking graves. An unmarked grave is like a hidden obstacle that makes people fail.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person who does not know a grave is there is 'blind' to it and may walk over it and become טמא. Leaving the grave unmarked is like putting a stumbling block in his way.

phrases.english: אביי said: From here:
"And before the blind you shall not put a stumbling block."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different source than the מצורע's call

steps.title: רב פפא: Pave, pave, clear the way
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא brings a פסוק from ישעיהו: 'Pave, pave, clear the way.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: 'And He will say: Pave, pave, clear the way.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives another hint for marking graves. The פסוק tells us to clear the road for people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Clearing the way means removing whatever could harm people on the road. A hidden grave is a danger of טומאה, so marking it is part of clearing the way.

phrases.english: רב פפא said:
"And He will say: Pave, pave, clear the way."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another alternative source, after אביי

steps.title: רב חיננא: Remove the stumbling block from My people's way
steps.stepSummary: רב חיננא brings the end of the same פסוק: 'Remove the stumbling block from the way of My people.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חיננא said: 'Remove the stumbling block from the way of My people.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב חיננא offers his own source. He uses the second half of the פסוק רב פפא just quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This half of the פסוק speaks openly about removing a מכשול from people's path. An unmarked grave is that kind of hidden danger.

phrases.english: רב חיננא said:
"Remove the stumbling block from the way of My people."
phrases.notes: This is the end of the same פסוק רב פפא just quoted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the second half of רב פפא's פסוק

steps.title: רבי יהושע בריה דרב אידי: Show them the way to walk
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בריה דרב אידי brings a פסוק from שמות: 'And you shall show them the way in which they must walk.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע the son of רב אידי said: 'And you shall show them the way in which they must walk.'
steps.whatsHappening: Another אמורא gives one more source for marking graves. Showing people the right way to walk includes warning them where graves are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק tells us to guide people on their path. Marking graves shows them where it is safe to walk without becoming טמא. The list of sources continues in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: And you shall let them know, show them

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי אָמַר:
phrases.english: רבי יהושע the son of רב אידי said:
"And you shall show them the way
in which they must walk."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another alternative source in the list, after רב חיננא
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות 18:20, 'והודעת להם את הדרך אשר ילכו בה'

steps.title: מר זוטרא's source: separate Israel from impurity
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא brings a פסוק from ויקרא that tells us to keep the Jewish people away from טומאה, which hints at marking graves.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא said: The source is "And you shall separate the children of Israel from their impurity."
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא adds another פסוק to the list of sources for marking graves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says to keep בני ישראל away from טומאה. Marking a grave does exactly that, because it warns people not to walk over it and become טמא.

phrases.english: Mar Zutra said:
"And you shall separate the children of Israel from their impurity."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another אמורא adds one more source to the list that began with אביי.
steps.raayaObject: The duty to mark graves so people do not become טמא

steps.title: רב אשי's source: make a safeguard for My charge
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reads "ושמרתם את משמרתי" as a command to build protective fences around the מצוות, and marking graves is one of those fences.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The source is "And you shall keep My charge," which means: make a safeguard for My charge.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives his own source and explains how he reads it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The double language, guarding a guard, teaches that we must put up safeguards so people do not come close to breaking a הלכה. Marking graves is such a safeguard, because it keeps people from getting טמא and then touching holy things.

keyTerms.meaning: My charge, what I commanded you to guard

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
"And you shall keep My charge"
make a safeguard for My charge.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another אמורא adds a source, this time with a short explanation of the פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: The duty to mark graves, seen as a protective fence

steps.title: רבינא's source: one who sets the way
steps.stepSummary: רבינא brings a פסוק from תהלים about someone who sets out the way, which hints at marking which paths are safe to walk on.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: The source is "And to him who sets the way, I will show the salvation of God."
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives the last source in the list for marking graves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Setting the way" is read as marking the roads, so people know which paths are טהור to walk on. This closes the list of אמוראים that started with אביי.

keyTerms.meaning: And he who sets (orders) the way

steps.whatToRemember: Many אמוראים give different פסוקים as hints for marking graves. They all agree on the הלכה and only differ on which פסוק hints at it.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
"And to him who sets the way, I will show the salvation of God."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The last אמורא in the list gives his source.
steps.raayaObject: The duty to mark paths and graves

steps.title: Whoever weighs his ways will see God's salvation
steps.stepSummary: Using the same פסוק, רבי יהושע בן לוי teaches that whoever carefully weighs his ways will merit to see the salvation of הקדוש ברוך הוא. He reads ושׂם as ושׁם.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: Whoever weighs his ways merits to see the salvation of הקדוש ברוך הוא, as it says "And sets the way." Do not read "ושׂם" (sets) but "ושׁם" (weighs): one who weighs the way, "I will show him the salvation of God."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a side lesson built on רבינא's פסוק. It is no longer about graves but about how a person should live.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן לוי uses an אל תקרי: by changing the dot on the letter, ושׂם (sets) becomes ושׁם (weighs, appraises). The lesson is that a person who stops to think about the right way to act is promised to see God's salvation.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not read it as... (a drasha that reads a word differently)

steps.confusionAlert: אל תקרי does not mean the פסוק's text is changed. The original reading stays, and the second reading adds an extra lesson.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
Whoever weighs his ways
merits and sees the salvation
of the Holy One, Blessed be He,
as it says: "And sets the way."
Do not read it as "vesam" (sets),
phrases.notes: The only difference is the dot on the letter: שׂ (sin) becomes שׁ (shin).

phrases.english: but rather as "vesham derech" (weighs the way):
"I will show him the salvation of God."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the פסוק רבינא just quoted and draws an aggadic lesson from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who carefully weighs his ways merits to see the salvation of הקדוש ברוך הוא.

steps.title: רבי ינאי's student who held back his questions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a story: רבי ינאי had a student who asked him hard questions every day but did not ask on the שבת of a festival.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי had a certain student who would ask him difficult questions every day, but on the שבת of a festival he would not ask him difficult questions.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a story connected to רבי יהושע בן לוי's lesson about weighing one's ways. It sets the scene, and the rest of the story comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On ordinary days the student challenged his רבי freely. On the festival שבת he held back, which is the behavior the story will go on to explain and judge.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yannai had
a certain student
who every day would ask him difficult questions,
but on the Shabbos of a festival
he would not ask him difficult questions.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יַנַּאי הֲוָה לֵיהּ הָהוּא תַּלְמִידָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a story that continues the theme of weighing one's ways.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Story setup: the student held back his challenges on the festival שבת.
